title: Scaling up vs scaling out
subtitle: A hot day at the ice-cream shop: one giant server or several regular ones?
mission: The school’s ice-cream shop sells through the app, and the heat peak (3 pm) reaches 2,000 orders per second. With the same money (R$ 800 a month), you can rent 1 xl machine or 4 m machines. At 3 pm, one machine burns out. Compare both choices and also find out when buying more machines stops helping.

predict.question: same cost: 1 xl machine (8 times stronger) or 4 m machines. At 3 pm one machine burns out. Who keeps selling ice cream?

options.four: The 4 m: losing one still leaves three
options.both: Both, since they cost the same

feedback.right: right! With 4 machines, losing one drops capacity from 3,200 to 2,400 orders/s, still above the 2,000 peak. The lone xl machine is a single point of failure: when it burns out, capacity goes to zero.
feedback.wrong: look at the chart: the 4 m machines drop from 3,200 to 2,400 orders/s at 3 pm and still cover the 2,000 peak. The lone xl has the same total power, but when it burns out there’s nobody left.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Run it and look at the capacity after the failure.

coach.ui: guess noted. Run with 4 m machines and look at the line after 3 pm.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run scale and look at the capacity after the failure.

tryNext.ui: Now use 10 xl machines and raise the peak to 8,000: see what becomes the bottleneck.
tryNext.cmd: Run scale --machines 10 --size xl --peak 8000 and see what becomes the bottleneck.

why.simples:
Scaling up (vertical) is swapping the server for a super-server: a bigger machine, with more CPU and memory. It’s simple, the code doesn’t even notice. But it has a ceiling (there’s no infinite server) and, if it gets sick, the shop closes.
Scaling out (horizontal) is hiring more identical servers and splitting the line among them. If one leaves, the others keep going. You can grow with almost no ceiling, but you need someone organizing the line (the load balancer, next lesson) and servers that keep nothing in their heads (stateless servers, lesson 1).
And careful: if every server scoops from the same freezer, hiring more people doesn’t help once the freezer is the slowest part. The bottleneck moves.
why.dev:
In the cloud, scaling up usually means restarting the machine at another size (minutes offline, unless another one covers), and sizes have a limit. Scaling out requires a stateless app: sessions, uploaded files and work queues live outside the server.
Autoscaling turns machines on by itself based on a metric (CPU, requests per second, queue length), but it takes time: it has to notice the rise, boot the machine, warm the app up and pass the health check. A peak that arrives in seconds (like a viral link) is over before help arrives, so keep headroom or schedule the increase before known events. And a rule of thumb: have N+1, enough capacity to survive losing one machine at peak.
why.especialista:
Scaling out isn’t linear forever. Everything shared (database, cache, a lock, a single queue) becomes the new bottleneck, and coordination between nodes costs: models like Amdahl’s Law and the Universal Scalability Law show the curve flattening, and sometimes going down, as contention grows. That’s why the next step is splitting state: read replicas, caches, partitioning (sharding) by key.
Autoscaling has traps too: flapping (scaling up and down nonstop, fixed with stabilization windows), account quota limits, cold starts, and scaling that worsens the bottleneck below (more servers = more connections to the same database). Scale on the metric that actually saturates, and test the peak before the day.

steps:
Create a folder escola-escala with two files. The compose.yaml:
name: escola
services:
  app:
    image: traefik/whoami
  lb:
    image: nginx:1.30
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - app

Start it with three replicas of app (scaling out):
docker compose up -d --scale app=3
Repeat curl http://localhost:8080 several times (in Windows PowerShell, curl.exe) and look at the Hostname line.

Go back to one replica. nginx looks up app’s addresses when it starts, so restart it:
docker compose up -d --scale app=1
docker compose restart lb
Repeat the curl: now the Hostname is always the same.
Shut everything down: docker compose down
recipe.ok: with 3 replicas, the Hostname alternates among three different values (the short ids of the app containers); with 1 replica and lb restarted, the Hostname no longer changes.
